messages.author: abab84dd2ba42997
messages.subject: Sampling error for Gaussian process model
parts:
Hi stan users,

I am attempting to implement a Gaussian Process logistic regression using stan. I am unfamiliar with these models so my implementation is probably wrong but I'm trying to get something fit in stan so I can play around and understand the models better. For this reason, I have written some pretty un-optimised code -- so that all the loops and assignments are clear to me, before I try to optimise (for example using the multivariate Matt trick and Cholesky decompositions).

In any case, the model I have right now compiles but then generates the following error in sampling:

Error in sampler$call_sampler(args_list[[i]]) : 
  boost::too_many_args: format-string referred to less arguments than were passed
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

It would be great if someone could point out the bug that's causing this. I've tried running stan with the c compiler in debug mode but this doesn't produce more informative output.

More generally, is there a way to declare a constrained object (such as the covariance matrix K) within the model block? I am not interested in the samples of K but in the samples of the hyperparameters nu, lambda and r, so therefore it seems like an unnecessary memory burden to store samples of K. However, if I just declare K to be an N by N matrix within the model block then I get errors that K is not positive definite. I suppose there's a better way to constrain the hyperparameters so that K is always positive definite but I'm not sure what this is.

Model and example data attached. Thanks as always for your help.

Tom

parts: On Tuesday, January 22, 2013 10:47:42 AM UTC-5, Tom Wallis wrote:

More generally, is there a way to declare a constrained object (such as the covariance matrix K) within the model block? I am not interested in the samples of K but in the samples of the hyperparameters nu, lambda and r, so therefore it seems like an unnecessary memory burden to store samples of K. However, if I just declare K to be an N by N matrix within the model block then I get errors that K is not positive definite. I suppose there's a better way to constrain the hyperparameters so that K is always positive definite but I'm not sure what this is.

The hyperparameters should be constrained so that the matrix is positive definite in theory, so double check that you implemented the formula right. Due to numerical imprecision, it may come out as indefinite. Do such errors cause the sampler to stop or just to reject the proposal? The latter isn't really a major problem.

I'm not sure about your other error message, but I remember something like this happening before when a transformation failed the respect the constraint on the transformed parameter's support, due to numerical issues.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Sampling error for Gaussian process model
parts:
On 1/22/13 12:44 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Tuesday, January 22, 2013 10:47:42 AM UTC-5, Tom Wallis wrote:
>
> More generally, is there a way to declare a constrained object (such as the covariance matrix K) within the model
> block?

Guaranteed constraint enforcement is only available
for parameters, and the covariance matrix for a GP needs
to be constructed, not sampled (though its hyperparameters
may need to be fit).

> I am not interested in the samples of K but in the samples of the hyperparameters nu, lambda and r, so
> therefore it seems like an unnecessary memory burden to store samples of K.
Right. You don't want to store samples of K.

> However, if I just declare K to be an N
> by N matrix within the model block then I get errors that K is not positive definite. I suppose there's a better way
> to constrain the hyperparameters so that K is always positive definite but I'm not sure what this is.
>
>
> The hyperparameters should be constrained so that the matrix is positive definite in theory, so double check that you

> implemented the formula right. ...

What you probably want to do is add what Radford Neal calls
jitter to the covariance function. Otherwise, if you have two data points
with identical x values, you won't get a positive definite covariance
matrix.

I coded up all the basic GP models in Stan for the next manual.
The models, sample data, and R code to run them through RStan are
available from our source-code repository here:

https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/#git%2Fsrc%2Fmodels%2Fmisc%2Fgaussian-process

It includes examples of how to generate from the prior, fit
hyperparameters, calculate the predictive distribution analytically,
and run logistic regressions.

And you can read a version of the latest doc (although not
with the usual fonts because it's done on our build machine) here:

http://d1m1s1b1.stat.columbia.edu:8080/job/Stan%20Manual/ws/doc/

I also added a chapter on measurement error models and meta-analysis,
and a chapter on mixtures/clustering models (soft K-means, naive Bayes,
LDA).

This will all be in the next release, which we hope to push out pretty
soon.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling error for Gaussian process model
parts:
Ah, now I see your model. Indeed, you want to use
jitter if you have identical inputs (or if you want to
fit a noisy regression rather than an exact one even
without identical inputs).

You should declare and define mu as transformed data,
not as a local model variable. We really need a zero_vector(N)
function to produce an N-vector filled with zeroes, or even
a general vector(x,N) to produce an N-vector filled with x.

The model will go faster if you vectorize operations
like the binomial sampling by precomputing the p vector.
That is, turn this:

for (n in 1:N) {
p[n] <- (gamma + (1 - gamma) * inv_logit( f_x[n] ));
y[n] ~ binomial(n_trials[n], p[n]);
}

into

for (n in 1:N) {
p[n] <- (gamma + (1 - gamma) * inv_logit( f_x[n] ));
}
y ~ binomial(n_trials, p);

We need to get busy vectorizing our basic functions so you could
just write

y ~ binomial(n_trails, gamma + (1 - gamma) * inv_logit(f_x));

Also, your covar function definition can be vectorized:

for (i in 1:N){
for (j in 1:N){
for (d in 1:D){
in_sum[d] <- ((x[i,d] - x[j,d]) / r[d]) * ((x[i,d] - x[j,d]) / r[d]);
}
K[i,j] <- nu * exp(-lambda * sum(in_sum));
}
}

Ideally, this would be written without the d loop by converting
to matrices and vectors and writing:

K[i,j] <- nu * exp(-lambda * dot_self((x[i] - x[j])/r));

- Bob

I'm trying to perform joint hyperparameter fitting and predictive inference, by fitting over two feature dimensions to data (25 cases), and predicting the output of the GP for 200 test cases (predictive inference). How will a model such as this scale with more data?

Note that I'm avoiding the analytical solution because I'm eventually moving to classification once I have this working satisfactorily.

Model and data file attached.

Best

Tom

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampling error for Gaussian process model
parts:
To answer the earlier question, it's still better to do the
Cholesky if you take more than one sample. The multi-normal
does a Cholesky decomposition inside, so if there's only
one sample taken per covariance matrix, there's no difference.

I don't think the test case locations are going to cause
problems, but I don't have a lot of experience with GPs.
If you could test this and report back, it'd help all of
us -- just run a test with new points inside instead of outside
the range of the training points.

You can see if there are rejected samples by just measuring
how many times the parameter vector returned by NUTS changes from
iteration to iteration. You can also look at the step size
and number of leapfrog steps (2^depth). If the number of steps
is consistently large across chains, it's a strong hint that the
geometry of the posterior is complicated.

- Bob

Hi Bob, 

Here are some test results. I'm running these on a macbook pro 2.3 GHz i7 (each chain in parallel). To reiterate, this is a two-dimensional Gaussian Process model, predicting a test set from a training set, with hyperparameters on the covariance function as given for the Automatic Relevance Determination equation on page 80 of the manual. The first dimension of x is a constant (for testing purposes). I am running 4 chains for 200 iterations (100 warmup). Data were generated with a set seed in R, but the seed was free in Stan.

Run 1 (see test_data_1): 

data: 
25 training points, z-scored y values, 50 test points that span the range of the training set.

results:

On Tuesday, January 29, 2013 6:11:43 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
To answer the earlier question, it's still better to do the
Cholesky if you take more than one sample.  The multi-normal
does a Cholesky decomposition inside, so if there's only
one sample taken per covariance matrix, there's no difference.

I don't think the test case locations are going to cause
problems, but I don't have a lot of experience with GPs.
If you could test this and report back, it'd help all of
us -- just run a test with new points inside instead of outside
the range of the training points.

You can see if there are rejected samples by just measuring
how many times the parameter vector returned by NUTS changes from
iteration to iteration.  You can also look at the step size
and number of leapfrog steps (2^depth).  If the number of steps
is consistently large across chains, it's a strong hint that the
geometry of the posterior is complicated.

- Bob
